title: Why Some Recipes Scale Badly
objective: After this level you can explain how the steps an algorithm needs grow as its input grows, and why that decides whether it is usable.
summary: Big O notation describes how an algorithm's steps grow with its input. Doubling the data adds one step, doubles or quadruples the work, and brute-force route checking grows so fast it is ruled out.

cards.headline: Two recipes give the same answer. Only one finishes.
cards.body: On a handful of items, every method looks instant. What matters is what happens as the input grows, and some methods grow so fast that trying every option is simply ruled out.

cards.headline: Count how steps grow, not seconds
cards.body: Computer scientists describe an algorithm's efficiency with big O notation: how its running time grows with the size of its input, called n. Constant factors are dropped, so reading a phone book two pages at a time is still O(n), just like reading one page at a time. It's the shape of the growth that counts, not the speed of today's machine.

items.label: O(n)
points: Linear search, one item at a time

cards.headline: When every option must be tried
cards.body: The traveling salesperson problem asks for the cheapest round trip through a set of cities. Trying every route is hopeless: n cities have (n-1)!/2 different tours. Five cities give 12. Ten cities give 181,440, and every added city multiplies the count again. That runaway growth rules out checking tours one by one, however fast the computer.

cards.headline: Growth: measured
learned: Big O describes how steps grow as the input grows
Doubling data: one more step, twice the work, or four times
Growth, not machine speed, decides if a method is usable

questions.prompt: Put these growth rates in order, from the one that grows slowest to the one that grows fastest.
questions.explanation: When the data doubles, O(log n) adds one extra step, O(n) takes twice the steps, and O(n squared) takes four times the steps.

questions.prompt: An O(n squared) method handles a list of 1,000 items. How does its work change for 2,000 items?
questions.explanation: For O(n squared), doubling the data multiplies the steps by about four.

questions.prompt: Why is binary search described as O(log n)?

options.label: Doubling the list adds only one more step
It checks every item exactly once
It compares every item with every other
It tries every possible order of the list
options.rationale: That's brute force, which grows far faster.

questions.explanation: Binary search halves the list each step, so doubling the list adds just one step: logarithmic growth.
